summary:
Kerala stands under India's national transgender-rights framework, which Parliament narrowed in March 2026. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill replaced the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinter and to intersex individuals; trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist, while the government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking. Critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. The Supreme Court decriminalised same-sex acts in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

Kerala's own machinery is constituted and measurably engaged. The state has a Transgender Welfare Board, one of the 12 states and union territories reported to the federal parliament in December 2021 as having set one up under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules. It registered 2 of the 7 national cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 and 4 of the 11 recorded in 2023, joint-highest with Tamil Nadu and among the largest sub-national totals in those years.

Those registration figures carry the source's own caveat. National recording is sparse, 20 cases across 2019-23, because of police registration bias, set against survey data showing 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence. Registered cases therefore show a system that at least accepts complaints, not a rarity of violence.

No state-specific restriction on gender identity, presentation or facilities is documented for Kerala. For a trans visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards were removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters is documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
tangentialFactors:
The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities.

The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic. That national assessment sits alongside the checkpoint incidents above, which involve federal forces rather than state police.

Kerala's case-registration totals rank with Tamil Nadu's as the highest sub-national counts in 2023, a comparison that reflects both complaint volume and recording practice rather than a measured difference in underlying violence.
localsOnly:
Residents of Kerala have access to a constituted Transgender Welfare Board operating under Section 10(1) of the 2019 Rules, one of only 12 such bodies reported to parliament in December 2021, and the state's police machinery records complaints under the Transgender Persons Act at rates among the highest in the country.

For residents, the March 2026 amendment's shift away from self-identification restricts who can obtain legal recognition, and trans people who self-identify outside the recognised socio-cultural categories fall outside the scheme regardless of where in India they live. Trans communities nationally report fear of a rise in assaults following the removal of gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in 2024.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable to residents, and no state-level relationship-recognition measure is sourced for Kerala.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the sources do not record how Kerala authorities are applying the March 2026 recognition rules in practice, including whether the state welfare board handles cases for people excluded by the amendment.

Unresolved: the 27.2% physical and 22.3% sexual violence prevalence figures come from national survey data and are not disaggregated to Kerala in the inventory; no state-level violence prevalence figure is sourced.

Unresolved: whether police registration bias in Kerala differs from the national pattern behind the 20 cases recorded across 2019-23 is not stated by the source, and no Kerala-specific checkpoint, custody or airport incident appears in the inventory. The documented checkpoint incidents come from other states and are cited as indicators of federal-force practice a visitor may encounter anywhere in India.
